_comment: Four rules in this feature exist in both C# and TypeScript, and every one of them
fails silently when the two drift:
- the grove's worth. The client draws it over the player's own grove and the server
puts it beside their name on a board. Disagree, and a player sees two different
numbers for one grove and has no way to tell which is real.
- the keeper level. It decides which companions count as earned rather than bought,
so a curve that disagrees moves value between the two halves of a score and past
- the public name. The client previews it in the rename panel; the server decides it.
Disagree, and a player is shown one name and published under another.
- the league, which is the star rating. It picks which board somebody is ranked on.
Assets/Game/Tests/GroveBoardTests.cs is the C# half; firebase/functions/test/grove.mjs
is the server half. Both read this file. Invariant 9a, for the boards.
The catalog below is written in homestead.json's own schema so the C# half can feed it
through HomesteadMapper — the mapper that ships — rather than through a second reader
_companionComment: The roster the worth cases are scored against, in the manifest's own shape.
A companion with no price is given away and is worth nothing, which is why monarch
never appears in an expected total however it is held. Everything else must be owned
outright to count: the unlock rule is keeper level AND purchase, so passing a gate
hands nothing over and a companion is in a grove only because it was paid for.
The gate is still read, and it is read before the clamp rather than inside it. A save
naming a companion whose gate its own keeper level has not reached cannot have come
about honestly, so the server drops that entry entirely — which is tighter than clamping
it. The client does not, and cannot: it is scoring holdings it knows to be real and a
purchase is permanent, so a companion kept through a gate retune stays held. Those cases
carry `serverOnly` and the C# half skips them, for the reason it skips a clamped one.
_worthComment: `affordable` is the ceiling on the bought half: everything the account could ever have
had to spend, derived by the server from the star ledger plus what it granted itself.
The client has no ceiling — it is scoring its own true holdings — so the C# half runs
only the cases whose clamp does not bite and which are not marked `serverOnly`.
`earned` is structurally zero now and every case says so. It was companions the keeper
ladder had reached, back when reaching a gate granted one; the rule is level AND
purchase now, so everything in a grove was bought and everything is clamped. The field
stays because the clamp is expressed in terms of the split and because a future reward
that genuinely is handed over belongs in it.
A home rung is gated the same way a companion is, and for the same reason: the ladder
became keeper level AND purchase, so a save naming a rung its own star ledger cannot
reach did not come about by playing. Dropped outright rather than cut down, which is
strictly tighter than the clamp — and the two directions are both pinned, because a
gate that never lets go is as wrong as one that never bites.

_starComment: The star ladder, which is the only thing a score is banded into now. The league ids it used to name went with the league board (see LeaderboardBoard); l0..l8 are spent.
_keeperComment: The keeper-level curve, in progression.json's own shape.
The client derives a level from XP to decide which companions are unlocked; since the
boards, the server derives one to decide which companions count as earned. The two
walks have to agree exactly — a level out by one moves a companion's whole price from
the earned half of a score to the bought half, where the clamp can then take it away.
Band boundaries are what these cases are for: 120 is the first level-2 XP and 119 is
the last level-1 XP, and the tail cases exercise the arithmetic past the authored
bands where the step grows by tailXpIncrement each level.
_nameComment: The public form of a stored name.
`public` is what both sides must produce from `stored`. `allowed` is server-only: the
word filter is not shipped in a client, because a list in a client is a list an attacker
reads out of the client. A name that is not allowed is not refused — the player keeps it
on their own screens and is published under a generated handle.
The bidi cases are the ones that matter most. U+202E re-orders the text that follows it,
so a name carrying one misdraws the rest of the row and sometimes the rows under it — a
defect a length cap and a word list both sail straight past, and the likeliest way a
public list of user-supplied strings gets broken.
`storedCodes` and `publicCodes` are the same two strings as UTF-16 code points, and they
are what the C# half reads. Unity's JsonUtility does not survive these strings: it
truncated `Fern‮Willow` at the escape, which silently shifted every expectation in
the array by one field and produced a failure that looked like a bug in the sanitiser.
The server half reads the strings and asserts the codes agree with them, so the two
encodings cannot drift — a vector file that disagreed with itself would be worse than
either encoding alone.
`key` is the collision key: what two names must share to be the same name, and the id
of the document that holds the reservation (functions/src/names.ts). Both sides must
produce it from `stored`, because the client folds to read the right document for its
'is this taken' hint and the server folds to decide the claim. A divergence there is a
wrong hint rather than a duplicate name — the transaction is still the authority — but
it is invisible from either side alone, which is what these vectors are for.
`claimable` is the pair of measurements together, and the cases that earn it are `!!`
and the middle dots: two visible characters, so the old rule published them, and an
empty fold, so nothing could ever reserve them. Two keepers would have stood on one
board under one name with nothing able to tell them apart.
`keyCodes` is `key` as UTF-16 code points, and it is there for `storedCodes`' reason:
Unity's JsonUtility cannot be trusted with these strings.
_catalogComment: The catalog the worth cases are scored against lives in grove-catalog.json beside this
file, in homestead.json's own schema and nothing else.
A file of its own rather than a block in here, so the C# half can hand it straight to
HomesteadMapper.TryRead — the reader that ships — instead of to a second reader written
for the test. A vector proved against a parser nobody uses proves nothing about the game.
_endlessComment: What the Infinite lane pays, derived twice and pinned here.
`endlessCases` is the only rule in this game that turns a save into XP without a star
behind it (invariant 9's one exception, see EndlessRewardTable). It runs in C# so the
game can draw a keeper level offline, and in functions/src/grove.ts so a published card
carries the same one — and when those two disagree nothing crashes and nothing is
refused: `buildCard` simply *drops* whatever the lower level gated (invariant 19a), in
silence, for the players who play the lane most.
Each case is a set of save rows and a config. `waves` is what both sides must read off
the rows; `xp` is what both must pay for it. The cases that matter most are the two
ceilings — a best is capped at 9,999 because it is published, a tally an order of
magnitude higher because it is a sum of bests — and the row cap, where a divergence
would only ever show up on an account somebody had tampered with.
`endlessDefaults` is what both sides use when no `endless` block has been published.
They agree on purpose rather than failing closed: a server that is a deploy behind would
otherwise publish every Infinite player short, with nothing said anywhere.
Written by Tools/make_endless_vectors.py — a third implementation, so a passing case
has been agreed by three copies that never read each other. Do not hand-edit.

_xpBoostComment: The XP boost's clamp, derived twice and pinned here.
A boost multiplies XP at the moment it is paid and banks the bonus, because XP is derived
and there is no running total to scale (invariant 9's second exception, see XpBoost). What
both runtimes then have to agree on is how much of that banked figure is real: it is
clamped to `provable x maxPercent%`, where provable is the star ledger's XP plus the
Infinite lane's. That is a *proportional* bound rather than a flat ceiling — a boost can
only ever have multiplied XP that was really paid — and it is the same shape groveWorth
uses to clamp a grove to what the account could afford (19a).
